evals.prompt: Sandbox note: this environment has Python but no GPU, no CUDA driver, no nsys binary and no network access; work only from what is supplied and do not install anything. Our ViT training job on one H100 only reaches about 44% GPU utilization. I already captured a steady-state profile and ran nsys stats and nsys analyze on it; the output is in /workspace/input/nsys-idle-gaps/nsys_report_summary.txt. evals.expected_output: The GPU is starved by the host: kernel queue times are near zero (QAvg about 1-2 us) and gpu_time_util reports 41-45% in-use regions. Causes: 77 MB host-to-device copies from pageable memory (~10 ms each, flagged by cuda_memcpy_async) and 412 cudaStreamSynchronize calls (~41 per iteration, 75.5% of CUDA API time) each after an 8-byte device-to-host copy, i.e. per-step .item()-style reads. Fix with pinned memory + non_blocking transfers and by removing/deferring the per-step syncs; then re-profile with sync attribution and re-run nsys analyze.
assertions: Concludes that the GPU is starved by the host rather than GPU-bound, citing the near-zero queue times in cuda_kern_exec_sum (QAvg about 1-2 us) and/or the 41-45% in-use regions reported by gpu_time_util.

Identifies the cuda_memcpy_async finding (77 MB host-to-device copies from pageable memory taking about 10 ms each) and recommends pinned host memory (DataLoader pin_memory=True or .pin_memory()) together with non_blocking=True transfers.

Identifies over-synchronization: 412 cudaStreamSynchronize calls (about 41 per iteration, 75.5% of CUDA API time), each preceded by an 8-byte device-to-host copy, consistent with per-step .item()/.cpu() reads, and recommends removing, deferring or batching them.
Every number it cites can be traced to the supplied nsys stats/analyze output; it does not invent timings or utilization figures.

Recommends a concrete nsys follow-up, such as re-profiling with attribution of the sync calls to source (CUDA or Python backtraces, or NVTX via --pytorch=autograd-nvtx with nvtx_kern_sum) and re-running nsys analyze (cuda_memcpy_async, cuda_api_sync, gpu_gaps/gpu_time_util) to confirm the fix.
Does not attempt to run or install nsys in the sandbox.

evals.prompt: Our 8x H100 DDP job (torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 train.py, NCCL backend) scales poorly: 8 GPUs give only 5.1x the single-GPU throughput. Using Nsight Systems, how do I collect per-rank profiles of a few steady-state iterations, check whether the NCCL all-reduces overlap with backward compute, and find a straggler rank? evals.expected_output: Collect one report per rank over a steady-state capture range, e.g. nsys profile -c cudaProfilerApi -t cuda,nvtx --pytorch=autograd-nvtx -o profile_%q{RANK} around the training processes, then run `nsys recipe nccl_gpu_overlap_trace -- profile_*.nsys-rep`, `nsys recipe nccl_gpu_time_util_map -- ...` and `nsys recipe cuda_gpu_time_util_map -- ...`, and compare per-rank cuda_gpu_kern_sum to spot the straggler.
assertions: Produces one report per rank using an output name that expands per rank (e.g. -o profile_%q{RANK}).
Restricts collection to a few steady-state iterations (e.g. cudaProfilerStart/Stop markers with -c cudaProfilerApi) instead of profiling the whole run.
Uses `nsys recipe nccl_gpu_overlap_trace` over the per-rank reports to measure NCCL/compute overlap.
Uses `nsys recipe nccl_gpu_time_util_map` and/or `nsys recipe cuda_gpu_time_util_map` across the rank reports to compare communication and compute utilization per rank.
Identifies stragglers by comparing per-rank kernel summaries (e.g. nsys stats -r cuda_gpu_kern_sum per rank, or nccl_sum) to find the rank whose compute runs longer while the others wait in NCCL.
